title: Show what the narrator makes the viewer imagine, on the word
when: Planning beats, cards, pictures and effects across a script.
summary: Walk the script sentence by sentence and ask what the narrator just made the viewer imagine; show that, on the word. Leave some sentences bare: a quiet stretch makes the next card land.
do: For each sentence, name what the viewer is imagining and put it on screen on the word that names it (within about 0.1 s).
Leave some sentences without a new card or effect so the next one lands.
Show only what the narrator said: nothing on screen claims what the voice did not.
Put a reaction (a meme, a joke beat) on or just after the punchline, never before it.
avoid: A new graphic on every sentence.
On-screen text that adds claims the narration never made.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Default to restraint: what top videos actually do
when: Deciding how many transitions, effects, zooms and inserts a video gets.
summary: Measured across top-performing reels, most cuts are hard cuts, shots last about three seconds, and audible effects are sparse and land on graphics rather than cuts. Restraint is the default; every extra device needs a reason.
do: Make most changes plain cuts (113 of 119 transitions in the measured reels were hard cuts).
Keep a median shot of about 3 s unless the style says otherwise.
Use about 0.4-0.9 audible effects per 10 s on graphics, not on cuts.
Hide a jump in the same picture with a short 0.2 s dissolve or a change of shot size, not a zoom on every cut; at most about three comic punch-ins a video.
avoid: A zoom or whoosh on every cut (owners find it annoying).
Several punchy transitions in a short video (two at most).
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: One card in the band, one thing in the reaction slot
when: Layering cards, captions, pictures and reactions.
summary: The screen carries one idea at a time: one card in its band and one thing in its reaction slot. A spoken list becomes typography, never a run of half-second clips.
do: Keep one card and one reaction on screen at a time.
Turn a spoken list into typography (a list builds on screen), not three 0.5 s pictures.
Use one character per idea and one shot per idea.
avoid: Captions colliding with cards.
One 0.5 s picture per noun.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Inserts sit in a frame; full screen is for the turn
when: Using photos, stock or footage inside a drawn or designed video.
summary: Pictures from outside the video's world sit inside a frame language (a polaroid, a card, a page, a phone) so the world stays one; full-screen inserts are kept for the turn. Each insert must show the line it sits on.
do: Frame inserts as polaroids, cards, pages or collage pieces; several framed stills beat many video cutaways.
Check every insert shows the words under it.
Grade an insert to match the video's world, never the other way round.
Keep stock video inside a frame unless the style is built on full-screen footage.
avoid: Full-screen stock strangers in a different colour world.
Fixed fees of inserts per minute ignored (about three a minute at most when a face or a main picture carries the video).
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Sound effect levels set against this voice
when: Setting sound effect levels, whooshes and impacts in a narrated video.
summary: Effects are mixed relative to the narrator's own loudness, not by hand: interface ticks sit lowest, whooshes a little higher, impacts higher still, and none ever louder than the voice. Voice loudness is fixed first; the finished mix is never lifted.
do: Fix the voice loudness first, then set effects relative to the voice's peak: interface sounds about -14 dB, whooshes -12, impacts -8.
Lead whooshes and hits: start them early so their peak lands on the cut or landing (within a few frames).
Put paper or prop foley on the landing frame and clicks on the action frame.
Duck music under every spoken line; under a freeze it almost disappears.
avoid: Effects louder than the voice.
Raising the whole finished mix into a limiter.
A sound effect on top of a spoken word; give it a pause.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: references/sound-and-memes.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: A style is a system, not a template
when: Defining or keeping a channel's look across many videos.
summary: A style that is a template makes every video the same edit. Write it as a system: the invariants that make it the style, a fixed house look, content slots that follow each script with a question that fills them, and a catalogue of the components each video used so the next one uses new ones.
steps: Write the thesis of the style in one sentence.
List the invariants that make it the style (never change).
Fix the house look: palette, type, captions, accents, framing.
Define slots that follow the content (the hook object, the turn, the source, the payoff) and the question that fills each from a new script.
Record which components each video used, and fill the next video's slots with components the last few did not use.
avoid: Pasting the previous video's scenes where the script does not call for them.
Changing the house look by accident.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: New components every video, the same house
when: Planning a video in a channel style that has made videos before.
summary: Videos in one style should feel like one channel without looking like copies: keep the house look and the invariants, and vary the components (props, card treatments, transitions, hook and outro devices) from video to video.
do: Before planning, look at which devices the last several videos used and pick ones they did not.
Keep the house look (type, captions, palette) fixed.
Register a new device when it is first used, so it is not repeated next time.
avoid: The same hook device, transition and outro in every video.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Every correction is taste, in the owner's own words
when: When the owner corrects an edit, a drawing or a style decision.
summary: When the owner corrects something ("too many zooms", "that sound is cheesy"), fix it and keep it as a rule in their own words, so the next video starts from it. The owner's words outrank the program's own learned rules; the current video's plan still wins.
do: Quote the owner's correction word for word when it becomes a rule.
Give the owner's rules priority over rules the program learned itself.
Read the owner's rules before planning the next video in the same style.
avoid: Paraphrasing the owner into a softer rule.
Letting an old rule override what this video's plan needs.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Captions that read: size, contrast and one keyword
when: Choosing caption looks and keyword highlights.
summary: Captions must be large and contrasting enough to read on a phone, never over the main subject, with one keyword per phrase lit when the style highlights words.
do: Keep captions at least about 48 px at 1080 wide and at least 3:1 contrast with what is behind them.
Highlight one keyword per phrase, chosen for meaning.
Put dark text on light accent colours (lime, yellow pills and tags).
Keep captions inside the platform's safe area and off the subject.
avoid: Small, low-contrast captions on a light background.
Em dashes in on-screen text.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Kinetic type devices and when each fits
when: Choosing an animated typography device for a beat.
summary: A small set of kinetic type devices covers most beats; each fits a kind of line, and each needs a reading hold after it lands.
do: Hook: the first 1.5-3 s line built big and fast.
Drum: a list or a repetition ("round and round") beaten out word by word.
Scramble: a word resolving out of letters, for a reveal or a name.
Flip stack: options flipping until one sticks.
Headline swap: "not X, Y" with the wrong word replaced by the right one.
Spring: a section title that pops into place.
Give each device a reading hold after it lands.
avoid: More than one or two of these per minute.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Study a reference edit from its frames, not an account of it
when: Learning a style from a reference video the owner provides.
summary: To match a reference edit, measure it: a contact sheet, frames every couple of seconds, a second-by-second log of what happens, then map every scene to a word time. Treat any AI's verbal account as a draft and check it against the frames.
steps: Sample the reference: a 1 fps contact sheet and full frames every 2 s.
Write a second-by-second log of cuts, cards, type and motion.
Check type, sizes and framing against the frames, not a description.
Write the style's invariants, house look and slots from what was measured.
Map each scene of a new video to its words, starting from the closest example.
avoid: Copying a model's summary of a reference ("57 swooshes, a yellow caption") without measuring it.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Check a style's prerequisite before planning
when: Choosing a named style for a video.
summary: Some styles need material the channel may not have (real screen recordings, one consistent world of footage). If it is missing, say what is missing and propose another style; never fill the gap with stock.
do: Before planning, name what the style needs and check it is there.
When it is missing, say so and offer the nearest style that works without it.
avoid: Filling a missing prerequisite with unrelated stock.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: SKILL.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Tactile paper: a talk told on printed paper, stop-motion
when: Paper-based videos, essays, history and ideas told on printed sheets (the Paper collage finish).
summary: Every noun becomes a physical sheet that unfurls, curls in or turns on its word; hand marks steer the eye; the paper moves on twos and the payoff on threes.
do: Make paper physical: every sheet enters, leaves and changes by a fold, curl or turn, never a fade or flat slide; every sheet has texture and a contact shadow.
Step designed motion on twos and the payoff on threes; keep reveals on the voice's clock.
Give every noun its own paper object on its word (a page, a print, a card, a map, a ticket); a drawn metaphor only when the line is abstract.
Let hand marks only steer the eye: a white arrow for look here, an underline under paraphrased printed words, an ellipse round the one thing named; marks stay glued to their paper.
Turn a page slowly to show the other side of an idea (before and after).
Bookend: the hook object returns with one new object that names the payoff.
Sound only where something enters or a section changes: a quiet bed, whooshes leading into pushes, foley on marks, one low boom under the big turn; 2.5-3.5 effects per 10 s.
avoid: A UI swoosh in place of a paper flip.
Floating marks not attached to paper.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/tactile-paper/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Kinetic doc: the narration made visible in an archive world
when: Documentary and history explainers with strong narration.
summary: Every word lands on screen as it is spoken in a black-and-white archive world with one red accent; pictures arrive as prints, windows and polaroids; punch lines get their own page.
do: Pop words on as spoken in one centred line: a big heavy word plus small words.
Keep the world black and white with one red accent.
Bring pictures in as prints, windows and polaroids.
Give each punch line its own page.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/kinetic-doc/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Data story: charts that draw themselves on paper
when: Lines that carry a quantity (prices, counts, growth, comparisons).
summary: When a line carries a quantity, cut to one cream paper sheet where a chart draws itself mark by mark in red and blue pencil, with handwritten notes; only real numbers, each with its source on screen.
do: Draw the chart mark by mark on the words, in pencil on paper.
Use only real numbers from the script or its sources, and show the source.
Annotate the point that matters by hand.
avoid: Invented or rounded-up numbers.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/data-story/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Telestrator: freeze on the key word and draw on it
when: Analysing a moment, a map, a scene or a picture like a sports breakdown.
summary: The picture plays, then freezes on the key word and gets drawn on like a sports replay: rings, marker arrows, zones and a rewind, always around the subject, never over a face.
do: Freeze on the word that names what to look at.
Draw rings, arrows and zones in a marker colour on the frozen frame.
Rewind or replay once to show the move again.
avoid: Drawing over a face.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/telestrator/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Halftone dossier: the story as a case file
when: Mysteries, true crime, profiles, investigations and secret histories.
summary: Every idea is one printed exhibit on cream paper: halftone pages in four flat inks, heavy misregistered headlines, stamps that slam and a profile card.
do: Treat each idea as one exhibit page.
Print in four flat inks with halftone dots and misregistered headlines.
Slam a stamp on the key finding.
Give the subject a profile card.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/halftone-dossier/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Swiss grid: the video as a poster programme
when: Clean, serious, design-led explainers and business videos.
summary: The frame is one modular page: a six-column grid, one typeface, one signal colour, key words laid out like a poster, a counter and exact quiet motion.
do: Lay everything on a six-column grid.
Use one typeface and one signal colour.
Set the key words as a poster composition.
Keep motion exact and quiet.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/swiss-grid/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Hologram HUD: scan the subject and read it like data
when: Technology, science, products, machines and anatomy explainers.
summary: The thing being talked about is scanned into a glowing wireframe; target boxes lock onto its parts and values roll in.
do: Scan the subject into a wireframe on the word that names it.
Lock target boxes onto its parts and roll in their values.
Keep the HUD around the subject, never over the main detail.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/hologram-hud/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: News package: one story as a news segment
when: Current events, explainers about a single story, rundowns.
summary: One package system: a sting that flies into the corner as the bug, a strap with a category tab, a split-flap board, schematic cards and a rundown of the points ticked off at the end.
do: Open with a sting that becomes the corner bug.
Use a strap with a category tab for each section.
Tick off the rundown of points at the end.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/news-package/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Step deck: tips as a numbered deck
when: List videos, tips, steps and how-to sequences.
summary: Every spoken word lands on its onset sized by how much it matters; each step opens on a card whose giant italic numeral shrinks into place; the picture switches every 1-2 s.
do: Open each step with a giant numeral that shrinks into place.
Size words by importance as they land.
Switch pictures every 1-2 s between cards, prints and line drawings.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/step-deck/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Product page: show the named thing, do not tell it
when: Reviews and explainers of a named tool, book, app or object.
summary: Every what or how line becomes a white page: the real picture, rebuilt interface and hairline drawings that a virtual camera moves through on the words, with two-tier headlines (heavy sans plus italic serif).
do: Build each line as a page the camera moves through.
Use hairline drawings and the real picture of the thing.
Set two-tier headlines: a heavy sans word and an italic serif word.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/product-page/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Vector explainer: one continuous world a camera travels
when: Animated explainers with a narrator and no footage.
summary: One continuous drawn world that a camera travels through, a subject that draws itself, serif headlines and word-reveal captions.
do: Build one continuous world and travel the camera through it instead of cutting.
Let the subject draw itself on its words.
Use serif headlines and captions revealed word by word.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/explainer-vector/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: Whiteboard: the thought is drawn while it is said
when: Whiteboard explainers (the Hand-drawn engine).
summary: Each sentence is drawn live in rough marker strokes with a visible marker following the stroke, handwriting for words, an eraser between pages, and the spoken word swept in colour in the captions.
do: Draw each thought while it is said, the marker visible on the stroke.
Wipe the board with an eraser between pages of ideas.
Sweep the spoken word in an accent colour in the captions.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/whiteboard/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.

title: A list read over pictures, the type doing the talking
when: List videos over pictures (places, observations, facts in a row).
summary: The voice names one observation every 4-6 s; one big word per line in an italic serif for mood or a heavy sans for facts, with a subline, word flashes and collage pages between.
do: Give each observation one big word plus a subline.
Use an italic serif for moods and places, a heavy sans for facts.
Change the picture with each observation, every 4-6 s.
source: ghost-editor (kurbaitaev, MIT), pinned ce17272: recipes/seoul-list/SYSTEM.md, restated in our own words for narrated faceless videos.
